pages.text: Consumer Expenditure Survey (CE) Consumer Expenditure Survey (CE) Skip Navigation Within Consumer Expenditure Survey (CE) Consumer Expenditure Survey (CE) The Consumer Expenditure Surveys (CE) program provides data on expenditures, income, and demographic characteristics of consumers in the United States. If you have been asked to participate in either the Consumer Expenditure Quarterly Interview Survey (Quarterly Interview) or the Consumer Expenditure Diary Survey (Diary), this site will help you verify that the survey came from the Census Bureau, verify that the person who called or came to your door is a Census Bureau employee, and inform you of how we protect your data. If you have additional concerns and wish to contact Census Bureau staff regarding the survey, please see the contact information at the bottom of this page. Overview The Consumer Expenditure Survey is a national survey conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau on behalf of the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The survey collects the data needed for the calculation of the Consumer Price Index (CPI), our nation’s most important measure of inflation. The Bureau of Labor Statistics has been conducting this survey since 1980. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Expenditure Survey website There are two separate surveys in the Consumer Expenditure Survey: the Quarterly Interview survey and the Diary survey. The Quarterly Interview survey asks household respondents questions about the costs of large purchases like cars or appliances and regular expenditures like rent, mortgage, insurance, or utilities. Controlling Wild Rodent Infestations Apr. 8, 2024 What to know Rodents can carry many diseases that can spread directly or indirectly to people. It's easier to control rodents before they can establish themselves in your home or building. Regularly check your home for rodent droppings and gnaw marks as these are both signs of a rodent's presence. Overview Rodents, such as rats, mice, and chipmunks, are known to carry many diseases. These diseases can spread to people directly, through: Handling of rodents Contact with rodent droppings (poop), urine, or saliva Rodent bites Rodent droppings, urine, and saliva can spread by breathing in air or eating food that is contaminated with rodent waste. Rodents can also carry ticks, mites, or fleas that can spread diseases. Many diseases do not cause any apparent illness in rodents. This means you cannot tell if a rodent is carrying a disease just by looking at it. Infestation of rodents in and around the home is the main reason disease spreads from rodents to people. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/publications/conversion-reported-temperatures-historical-scales-its-90 PUBLICATIONS Conversion of Reported Temperatures from Historical Scales to the ITS-90 Published October 26, 2026 Author(s) Allan Harvey Abstract While the International Temperature Scale of 1990 (ITS-90) has been a standard for many years, there is a large amount of historical thermophysical data reported on other scales. The differences of these scales from ITS-90 is typically small, but not necessarily negligible for reference-quality work. We describe conversion to ITS-90 from 34 different scales. These include not only the relatively well-known International Temperature Scales from 1968, 1948, and 1927, but also scales that have been used for cryogenic work at temperatures below the ranges of the older international scales, including the many scales that were based on the vapor pressure of helium. Scales specific to certain laboratories are also considered. Python code has been made available for the conversions described here. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry. But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel. "In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day." Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes. From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels. Sean Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem that led to air traffic controllers suspending take-offs for four hours on Friday had been caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades or faulty equipment. Though the ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, it had a knock-on effect on air travel on Saturday as airlines attempted to clear a backlog of flights. Officials including Duffy had previously attributed the issue to outdated equipment. Maintenance on US air traffic control systems was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre-optic cable by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider, Duffy said. And More Questions From Our Readers Skip to main content Could different backyard birds, such as a robin and a bluebird, produce viable offspring? Marilyn Foehrenbach Wirtz Could different backyard birds, such as a robin and a bluebird, produce viable offspring? Joseph Niemoeller | Glen Carbon, Illinois Although closely related species can have offspring, they typically don’t. Robins and bluebirds may be able to hybridize (there are no documented cases), but they have different plumages, songs, foraging habits and nest types, so it would be unlikely for them to choose each other. Such differences, along with geographic range and habitat preferences, prevent species from interbreeding even when it’s possible. Some species, like mallard ducks, do hybridize frequently. But the hybrid young may be a “dead end,” since they may be less likely to survive to adulthood or find their own mates. And More Questions From Our Readers Skip to main content Could a private citizen get hold of a genome and use it to bring an extinct animal back to life? Tracy Walker Could a private citizen get hold of a genome and use it to bring an extinct animal back to life? —Anjali Rawal | Encinitas, California There’s currently no way to bring an animal back from extinction based on genomic sequences alone. However, some lab groups and individuals hope to “bring back” extinct animals—including mammals, birds and amphibians—by modifying the genome of an existing species so the animal resembles an extinct relative and plays a similar ecological role. For instance, scientists with the Revive & Restore project have proposed using gene manipulation to create elephants that have the heavy coats of woolly mammoths. The same types of methods can be applied to currently endangered species; for example, adding genes to help a species cope with rising heat or survive an infection from an invasive pathogen. There are laws governing this kind of work. Can artificial intelligence help do it better? Knowable Magazine Schizophrenia is difficult for psychiatrists to diagnose. Can artificial intelligence help do it better? Knowable Magazine Schizophrenia is tough to diagnose. Patients may present with hallucinations (sometimes), social withdrawal (maybe) or delusions (not always). More generally, they just sound unlike themselves. Clinicians rely on their expertise and subtle cues to determine how different patients’ speech is, along with which symptoms appear over time, to justify leaning toward schizophrenia rather than another mental illness. This leads to delays in diagnosis. Americans with psychotic disorders—more than three million of whom have schizophrenia— receive a diagnosis a year and a half, on average, after their first symptoms appear. Researchers are now investigating whether artificial intelligence could improve diagnosis and care by listening to and analyzing what clinicians can’t hear or quantify, even if the software is working off just a few minutes of conversation. pages.text: Could T. rex swim? Kinda | National Geographic SCIENCE Could T. rex swim? Kinda Evidence suggests dinosaurs like tyrannosaurs were probably best suited to a version of the doggy paddle. Despite what's depicted in movies and books, the real Tyrannosaurus rex was likely an awkward swimmer at best. Illustration by Fotokita, Getty Images By Riley Black Published July 2, 2025 When Michael Crichton released the novel Jurassic Park in 1990, he included a terrifying chase through one of the park’s ponds. Fictional paleontologist Alan Grant, looking after kids Lex and Tim, tries to sneak by a dozing Tyrannosaurus rex and motor across a lake away from the dinosaur. The T. rex follows, swimming after them like “the biggest crocodile in the world.” The scene stood out so much that it’s been revamped for the new movie Jurassic World: Rebirth . But while tyrannosaurs might swim in movies and books, could they swim in real life? Carnivorous dinosaurs are not generally thought of as good swimmers. During much of the 20 th century, in fact, paleontologists wrongly assumed that herbivorous dinosaurs ran into rivers and lakes to avoid the jaws of T. rex , Allosaurus , and other predators. No one had found any direct evidence that such carnivores could swim. But the discovery of dinosaur swim tracks at fossil sites around the world have indicated that theropod dinosaurs—the group that contains T. rex , birds, and their relatives—were more aquatically adept than suspected and may have even done their own version of the doggy paddle. pages.text: Could the Way You Chew Food Affect Your Dementia Risk? | National Geographic Premium HEALTH Could the Way You Chew Food Affect Your Dementia Risk? Tooth loss has been linked to dementia and cognitive decline. Now researchers are uncovering why jaw health may matter more than we realize. Chewing engages parts of the brain involved in memory, and studies have linked tooth loss to a higher risk of dementia. Now researchers are exploring whether losing the ability to chew effectively could help explain that connection. Rebecca Hale, NGM Staff By Hadia Zainab Published November 13, 2026 Losing teeth may affect more than a person's ability to eat comfortably. Growing research has linked tooth loss to cognitive decline and dementia, although scientists are still trying to understand the reasons behind this connection. A 2026 review of 21 longitudinal studies involving about 35.7 million people found that tooth loss was associated with a higher risk of dementia and mild cognitive impairment, with the risk increasing as more teeth were lost. Researchers have proposed different explanations. Oral disease may not be the only factor; the loss of chewing ability itself could also play a role. Still, these findings do not establish a clear cause-and-effect relationship. “The relationship may work in several ways. pages.text: Could This Dutch Invention Help Tackle Plastic Pollution in America's Waterways? Skip to main content A Bubble Barrier creates a diagonal line of whiter water in Amsterdam's Westerdok. The Great Bubble Barrier Amsterdam’s Westerdok looks like many other outlets to the city’s historic canals. But look past the familiar boats and birds, and there is a distinct pattern in the water not found elsewhere in the city: a diagonal line of whiter water. That’s because an innovative “curtain,” known technically as a Bubble Barrier, lies below the surface. On the bottom of the waterway is a perforated tube which pumps air out, directing plastic to the surface. The natural flow of water then carries plastic litter to the Bubble Barrier’s catchment system, an aluminum trap on one side of the waterway, to prevent it from making its way to the North Sea. “Anything you can think of that people have in the city, we’ve seen here,” Philip Ehrhorn, co-founder and chief technological officer of the Great Bubble Barrier , the company behind the technology, told me as we surveyed the barrier on a warm day in September. The current catch—laminated restaurant menus, food wrappers, even a selfie stick—demonstrated that well. Westerdok’s Bubble Barrier was the company’s first, installed in 2019. Petersen | Granite Bay, California There is certainly a lot of energy when a volcano erupts—and I do mean a lot . As an example, the thermal energy released during the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens was enough to power the entire world for about two and a half days. Unfortunately, we cannot capture that energy. But we can capture some of the geothermal energy from magma cooling underground. In places where cooling magma is close enough to the Earth’s surface, we can drill wells and then circulate the hot water to either heat buildings directly or generate electricity. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/blogs/taking-measure/count-nist-provide-well-measured-holiday-cheer Taking Measure Just a Standard Blog Count on NIST to Provide Well-Measured Holiday Cheer December 22, 2025 By: Robin Materese Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email Credit: B. Hayes/NIST ’Tis the season to be … measure-y? During the holiday season, we measurement geeks can’t help but ask — and seek the answers to — some very important holiday-related questions. How long would it take Santa to visit every household in the U.S. with a child under the age of 18 if he spent approximately five minutes delivering presents to each house? pages.text: County-level Model-based Estimates from 2019 American Housing Survey: Signs of Rodents County-level Model-based Estimates from 2019 American Housing Survey: Signs of Rodents Skip Navigation County-level Model-based Estimates from 2019 American Housing Survey: Signs of Rodents January 15, 2024 The 2019 County-level Model-based Estimates from the 2019 AHS provides county estimates of rodent sightings for all counties in the United States. The American Housing Survey (AHS), sponsored by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), provides national, state-level, and select MSA-level information on housing characteristics, quality, and cost. Using the 2019 AHS, auxiliary data sources, and small area estimation methods, the experimental estimates provide measures for rodent sightings in occupied housing units for all U.S. counties. The experimental data file includes, for all U.S. counties: the estimated number of housing units from the 2019 Population Estimates Program (PEP), the number of occupied housing units which experienced a rodent sighting in a 12-month period between 2018-2019, and the 90 percent confidence interval for each estimate.
